solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Rand maybe in transmission of data? One's choice no longer

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside that other's letters

blocks.note: DT is the standard abbreviation for data transmission
Ayn Rand, the novelist, so Rand is an example surname whose first name is wanted

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the South African currency features in data transmission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rand' looks like the currency; 'maybe' signals that it is the writer Ayn Rand. DAYNT is an obsolete form of dainty.
explanation.definitionFit: Dainty once meant choice or excellent, and DAYNT is an obsolete spelling of it, hence the label 'no longer'.

clue.text: Able to see clearly again (chains tended to be loosened)

indicators.note: chains that are loosened fall apart, so the letters are freed into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words used together

explanation.surface: Someone freed from chains that had been carefully kept on them can see clearly once more.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed wordplay works with the definition: being released from a spell is like having chains loosened.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone disenchanted has been freed from an illusion or spell, so they now perceive things as they really are.

clue.text: Being a primate, he turned up with ordinary, entering a school

indicators.note: in a down entry, something turned up is read from the bottom, so backwards
going into something means being placed inside the letters of what follows

blocks.note: taken as written
a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
taken as written, then reversed
O is the standard abbreviation for ordinary

explanation.surface: A monkey-like male is turning up at a perfectly ordinary school.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -hood names a state or condition, so the word means the condition of being an ape.

clue.text: Company sent up king causing some laughter in theatre

indicators.note: in a down entry, something sent up runs from bottom to top, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: Coy is a military abbreviation for company
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A theatre company mocking a monarch gets the audience laughing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' reads like mockery in the theatre, but it only turns the company backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A yock (or yuck) is showbusiness slang for a laugh, especially a loud one from an audience.

clue.text: Wooden bit of tableware shunned by upper-class

indicators.note: what is shunned is kept away, so the named letter is left out

blocks.note: a tureen is a deep serving dish for soup
U is the standard label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: A wooden piece of tableware is looked down upon by posh diners.
explanation.definitionFit: Treen means made of wood, and as a noun it names small wooden household articles.

clue.text: Grand, in the manner of sporting occasion

blocks.note: G is slang shorthand for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
à la is French for in the manner of

explanation.surface: Something grand in the style of a big sporting day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' completes the phrase 'in the manner of' on the surface but works only as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a festive occasion, and in Britain often a sports meeting such as a swimming gala.

clue.text: Bird in Shakespeare supposedly arrived in doubled piece of muslin

indicators.note: a piece of a word is a part of it, here its centre portion
a piece of cloth doubled over folds round whatever sits between its ends

blocks.note: the central two letters of the six-letter word
came means arrived

explanation.surface: A bird from Shakespeare is said to have turned up wrapped in folded muslin.
explanation.walkthrough: Scamel appears once, in The Tempest; it may be a misprint, which is why the clue says 'supposedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Caliban promises to fetch 'young scamels from the rock', usually taken to be some shore bird.

clue.text: Emperor (Queen included) that's taken up an alias (7, two words)

indicators.note: something included is put inside the word around it
in a down entry, being taken up means reading from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: Emp. is the abbreviation for emperor
Queen Anne, the British monarch

explanation.surface: An emperor, with a queen in tow, has adopted a false name.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen name is a pseudonym used by a writer, which is a kind of alias.

clue.text: Extra Scotch, medium dry

blocks.note: M is the clothing-size abbreviation for medium
to air washing is to dry it

explanation.surface: An order at the bar: another Scotch whisky, medium dry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a drink order; 'Scotch' actually marks the answer as a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Mair is the Scots form of more, meaning extra or additional.

clue.text: String-pullers formerly? I'm not one that's devious about money

indicators.note: something devious takes a winding course, so the letters stray from their order
being about something means surrounding it

blocks.note: the letters of the phrase used together
M is a standard abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: Someone denies being a crooked operator in financial matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'String-pullers' suggests manipulators, which suits the denial; here it means puppeteers.
explanation.definitionFit: A motion-man was an old term for a puppeteer, who works the strings of a puppet show or motion.

clue.text: Tincture seen in coloured glow, a rich orange

indicators.note: something seen in another word is placed within its letters

blocks.note: an aura is a glow or halo of light
or is the heraldic tincture gold

explanation.surface: A heraldic colour shows up in a glowing halo of rich orange.
explanation.walkthrough: Tinctures are the colours of heraldry; or is gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Aurora is listed as a colour name for a rich orange, after the glow of dawn.

clue.text: Left to rest, soldiers during rest disturbed getting discharges

indicators.note: left to rest means one piece is attached to the next
something disturbed is thrown out of order
happening during something puts these letters inside it

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
to ease is to rest
soldiers, as in officers and men
the second rest is taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Troops are left to rest, their leave disrupted as they are discharged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' appears twice: once meaning ease, once as the letters to be rearranged around the rest of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A releasement is an old word for a release, so releasements are discharges or liberations.

clue.text: Spongy, running inside, like Pyramus' eyes?

indicators.note: one thing inside another sits within its letters

blocks.note: porous means full of holes, like a sponge
a race is a running contest

explanation.surface: Someone asks if Pyramus had spongy, streaming eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: In A Midsummer Night's Dream Thisbe laments Pyramus: 'His eyes were green as leeks.'
explanation.definitionFit: Porraceous means leek-green, from Latin porrum, leek, which fits Thisbe's description of Pyramus.

clue.text: Boiled leeks containing slice of conference pear

indicators.note: boiled vegetables are cooked and broken down, so the letters are reworked
containing means holding something inside
a slice of a word is a small part of it, here the opening letter

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the first letter

explanation.surface: A recipe of boiled leeks with a slice of Conference pear.
explanation.walkthrough: Conference is a well-known British pear variety, which makes 'conference pear' read as one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seckel is a small, sweet American pear variety.

clue.text: Cavity's rent a molar? More treated with this

indicators.note: something treated is worked on and changed, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of the three words together
taken as written; these letters plus the answer make up the anagram

explanation.surface: A dentist's riddle: is a split molar a sign of a cavity, best treated with this?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads backwards: MORE treated with the answer would give the letters of 'rent a molar', so take MORE out of those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Antral is the adjective from antrum, a body cavity such as a sinus, so it means relating to a cavity.

clue.text: Racket, deviously subtle vehicle for campaigning Brexiteers?

indicators.note: acting deviously means going by a crooked route, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: a racket is a bat used in tennis or squash
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A sly racket involving the campaign coach of the Leave side.
explanation.walkthrough: A battle bus is the coach a party tours in during a UK election; the Leave campaign's bus was notorious for its slogan.
explanation.definitionFit: Battle bus is British slang for the campaign coach that carries a party leader around during an election.

clue.text: Vertebrate of a kind from America I included in observation

indicators.note: being included in something means going inside it

blocks.note: Am. is the abbreviation for America
a note is a remark or observation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A particular backboned creature from America is noted in a field report.
explanation.definitionFit: Amniotes are vertebrates (reptiles, birds and mammals) whose embryos develop inside an amnion membrane.

clue.text: Always having to turn in, the moment causing irritation for the poet

indicators.note: turning something around means reading it the other way
turning in puts these letters inside the following word

blocks.note: for the nonce means for the present moment
ay (or aye) is an old word for always

explanation.surface: A poet is irritated at always having to go to bed at the moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Noyance is Spenser's shortened form of annoyance, hence an irritation in poetic usage.

clue.text: Claret vessel: a little left after meal imbibed by those that shouldn't?

indicators.note: something imbibed is taken in, so these letters go inside the others

blocks.note: Alcoholics Anonymous, for those who shouldn't drink
an ort is a scrap of food left over

explanation.surface: Wine from a decanter: leftovers drunk by people who ought not to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Claret' looks like the wine but is old slang for blood, so the vessel is a blood vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The aorta is the main artery from the heart, the chief vessel for blood.

clue.text: Hip flask of yesteryear bedecked corslet

indicators.note: something bedecked is dressed up and altered in appearance, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An old pocket flask decorated with a piece of body armour.
explanation.definitionFit: A costrel is an old flask or bottle with ears for hanging from the hip or belt.

clue.text: Food crop? After climbing tree one misses nothing (7, two words)

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading upwards, so backwards
something that misses a letter goes without it

blocks.note: the alder is a tree
taken as written
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A farmer asks if climbing a tree means losing the crop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Food crop' looks agricultural; the crop is the part of a bird's gullet, and the question mark admits the stretch to the throat.
explanation.definitionFit: Red lane is a colloquial term for the throat, the passage that food goes down, like a bird's crop.

clue.text: Last jam? Shame to open it

indicators.note: when one thing opens another it gets in among its letters

blocks.note: to jam or block is to clog
a sin is a shameful act

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that it is a pity to open the final jar of jam.
explanation.definitionFit: Closing means final, as in the closing stages or closing remarks.

clue.text: Flowerbed came back to life with grass curtailed

indicators.note: curtailed means having its tail cut, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: rose, as in rose from the dead
rye is a cereal grass

explanation.surface: A garden bed revived once its grass was cut back.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosery is a rose garden or a bed planted with roses.

clue.text: Woman, twice married, breaking cover, causing confusion locally

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for woman
hele is a dialect verb meaning to cover or hide
M for married, given twice

explanation.surface: A woman with two marriages behind her blows her cover and causes chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: Whemmle is a Scots and northern dialect word for an overturning, and so a state of confusion.

clue.text: West Dorking church showing place of origin?

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for west
a Dorking is a breed of domestic hen
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church in West Dorking reveals where something came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorking is a town in Surrey, but also gives its name to a breed of chicken.
explanation.definitionFit: Whence means from what place, and as a noun a source; the question mark marks the stretch.

clue.text: Bill, aged, shivering like poor Tom (tragically)

blocks.note: ac. is the abbreviation for account, a bill
aged means old

explanation.surface: An elderly man called Bill is shivering, just like Poor Tom in the play.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear, Edgar disguised as Poor Tom repeats 'Tom's a-cold'.
explanation.definitionFit: Acold is an archaic word for feeling cold, used by Edgar in his Poor Tom disguise in King Lear.

clue.text: Cavities requiring return of doctor, no longer healthy

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: holes are cavities
MO is a medical officer

explanation.surface: Tooth cavities need a trip back to the doctor, so they are no longer healthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer healthy' reads like sickness, but 'no longer' marks an obsolete spelling of a word meaning healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Holesom is an obsolete spelling of wholesome, meaning health-giving or sound.

clue.text: Splat – I'll dive in. Jock's reluctant

indicators.note: I will dive in: diving into something means going inside it

blocks.note: a splat is a thin strip of wood, as in a chair back, so a lath
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Scot hesitates before diving in with a splash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jock' is a nickname for a Scot, so the answer is a Scots word. 'I'll' is I will, so the I does the diving.
explanation.definitionFit: Laith is the Scots form of loath, meaning unwilling.

clue.text: Quite pooped (as once)? Take a nap round opportune time

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it

blocks.note: to nod off is to take a nap
sele is an old word for a good or opportune time, a season

explanation.surface: Totally exhausted, someone takes a nap at a convenient moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pooped' looks like tired, but poop once meant to befool; 'as once' flags the old sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Noseled means led by the nose, so thoroughly fooled, which matches the old verb poop, to cheat or deceive.

clue.text: Bother – nearly late, lift needed

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in a down entry, lifting a word turns it upwards, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: tardy means late

explanation.surface: Someone running late exclaims in annoyance that they need a ride.
explanation.definitionFit: Drat and bother are both mild exclamations of annoyance.

clue.text: When it's missing leg, inclined to go for big hit

indicators.note: a word that is missing something lacks those letters

blocks.note: sloping means inclined
pin is slang for a leg

explanation.surface: A cricket tip: when a batsman lacks the leg side, they're inclined to swing hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg' looks like the cricket field side; it is a slang word for a leg, pin.
explanation.definitionFit: To slog is to hit the ball hard and wildly, especially in cricket.

clue.text: Creon, or the edict he issued?

blocks.note: taken as written
Creon's edict was a ban on burying Polyneices

explanation.surface: Asks whether Creon is known for himself or for his famous decree.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sophocles' Antigone, Creon, king of Thebes, bans the burial of Polyneices; Antigone defies it.
explanation.definitionFit: Creon ruled Thebes in the Oedipus legend, so he is an example of a Theban, a native of that city.

clue.text: Beast reminding one of Hitler, equipment stuff being one short!

indicators.note: falling one short means a single letter is lacking at the end

blocks.note: rig is gear or equipment
to line, as in lining one's pockets, is to stuff

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a creature, its gear lacking one item.
explanation.walkthrough: The wartime song claimed Hitler had only one testicle, which explains the 'one short' joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A riglin is a male animal with an undescended testicle, recalling the song about Hitler's 'only one ball'.

clue.text: Shortening not in a crust? It ruins more than one of these

indicators.note: ruining something wrecks its form, so the letters are scrambled
the scrambled letters give a plural, so the answer is that word less its plural ending

blocks.note: the letters of the four words together

explanation.surface: A baker asks whether fat should go outside the pastry, where it spoils things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortening' looks like baking fat. The rearranged letters make the plural, 'more than one of these', so the singular drops the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: Truncation is the act of cutting something short, a shortening.

clue.text: Some times are bewildering by the sound of it

indicators.note: judging by the sound means the spoken word is wanted, not its spelling

blocks.note: to daze is to bewilder

explanation.surface: Some periods seem confusing, apparently.
explanation.definitionFit: Days are units of time, so a set of days is some times.

clue.text: Yearlings stop joining gee-gees

indicators.note: joining means one piece is attached to the next

blocks.note: ho is an old call to stop or halt
gee-gee is a child's word for horse, written GG

explanation.surface: Young animals stop and join up with the horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoggs are young sheep in their first year, before their first shearing.
